content.caveat: The existence and uniqueness of halves depend on the ambient algebraic structure.
content.exact: Given a structure with an addition operation, y is a half of x when y+y=x. A unique halving operation x↦x/2 exists only in contexts where this equation has exactly one solution y for each x under consideration.
content.example: In the real numbers, half of 7 is 7/2. In the integers, 7 has no integer half. In arithmetic modulo 5, 2 has a unique multiplicative inverse 3, so division by 2 is well-defined.
content.human: “Half of x” is not one universal operation. It depends on what x is and which operations exist in its mathematical structure.

assumptions: A group G acts on X.
H is an index-2 subgroup of orientation-preserving transformations.
r is any element of G\H.

content.caveat: Chirality is relative to a declared transformation group and an orientation-preserving subgroup; it is not an intrinsic word without that context.
content.exact: For x in X, define the mirror image r·x. The object x is chiral relative to (G,H) iff r·x is not in the H-orbit H·x. Because H has index 2, the property is independent of which r in G\H is chosen.
content.example: Left and right hands are the usual physical analogy: a mirror swaps handedness, while rotations alone do not.
content.human: A chiral object has a handedness: mirroring changes it in a way that allowed orientation-preserving motions cannot undo.

content.exact: For a set X, a relation ~ on X is an equivalence relation iff (i) for every x in X, x~x; (ii) for all x,y in X, x~y implies y~x; and (iii) for all x,y,z in X, x~y and y~z imply x~z.
content.example: Congruence modulo 2 partitions the integers into the even and odd equivalence classes.
content.human: A relation is an equivalence relation when it behaves like equality with respect to reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity.

content.caveat: Changing the transformation family changes which quantities qualify as invariants.
content.exact: I:X→Y is invariant under G iff for every g in G and x in X, I(g·x)=I(x).
content.example: The Euclidean distance between two points is invariant under rigid motions applied to both points.
content.human: An invariant deliberately forgets changes that the chosen transformations are allowed to make.

content.exact: For n in Z: n is even iff there exists k in Z with n=2k. n is odd iff there exists k in Z with n=2k+1.
content.example: 18 is even because 18=2·9. 19 is odd because 19=2·9+1.
content.human: Every integer belongs to one of two classes: even or odd.

content.caveat: Continuous functions, group actions, tilings, and dynamical systems use related but context-specific notions of periodicity.
content.exact: A sequence (a_n) is periodic with period p>0 iff a_{n+p}=a_n for every index n for which both terms are in the domain. A least positive such p, when it exists, is called the fundamental period.
content.human: A periodic sequence repeats exactly after some fixed positive number of steps.

content.caveat: This seed record uses the standard positive-integer definition; “prime elements” in general rings require separate contextual definitions.
content.exact: For p in Z with p>1, p is prime iff for every positive integer d, d divides p implies d=1 or d=p.
content.example: 7 is prime. 12 is not prime because 3 divides 12 and 3 is neither 1 nor 12.
content.human: A prime cannot be factored into two smaller positive integers greater than 1.

assumptions: F:T^k→X is periodic in each angular coordinate, where T=R/(2πZ).
ω in R^k is a frequency vector.

content.caveat: “Quasiperiodic” has other precise meanings in tilings, symbolic dynamics, cocycles, and other areas. Those require separate records rather than silently reusing this definition.
content.exact: In this record, f:R→X is quasiperiodic when f(t)=F(ω_1 t,...,ω_k t) for a function F on the k-torus and a frequency vector ω whose components are rationally independent: if m in Z^k and m·ω=0, then m=0.
content.example: f(t)=cos(t)+cos(sqrt(2)t) is a standard quasiperiodic example under this convention.
content.human: Quasiperiodic motion can be built from several periodic motions whose frequencies never line up into one common period.

content.human: A recurrence describes how values are linked across index steps. It need not always determine a unique sequence unless enough initial data and uniqueness conditions are supplied.

content.caveat: Sensitivity alone is not a universal definition of chaos.
content.exact: T has sensitive dependence on initial conditions iff there exists δ>0 such that for every x in X and every ε>0 there exist y in X and n>=0 with d(x,y)<ε and d(T^n(x),T^n(y))>δ.
content.example: In chaotic systems, small initial discrepancies may become macroscopically separated under iteration.
content.human: Sensitivity formalizes one kind of error amplification: no matter how closely two starting states are chosen, some nearby state can eventually move a definite distance away.

content.caveat: Symmetry depends on the chosen object representation and transformation group.
content.exact: The symmetry group of x relative to the action of G on X is Stab_G(x) = { g in G : g·x = x }.
content.example: A square in the Euclidean plane has rotations and reflections that map the square to itself.
content.human: Symmetry is never just “looks the same”: one must specify which transformations are allowed and what counts as unchanged.

content.caveat: Popular descriptions such as “random-looking” or “small errors grow” are not by themselves mathematical definitions of chaos.
content.exact: QEVA Protocol 0.1 assigns no universal predicate Chaos(T). A record claiming chaos must identify a contextual criterion (for example a named topological, measure-theoretic, symbolic, or metric definition) and state its hypotheses.
content.example: A map may satisfy sensitive dependence while failing some stronger named chaos criterion.
content.human: “Chaos” has several rigorous definitions. QEVA should name the definition being used instead of treating the word as self-explanatory.
